That’s the sentence. Worth counting how many places it turned up today, because it’s more
than it feels like:

Fede’s PQ companion check — a bare bool hid a real security bug: a retired-but-
unanchored key read as authorized, because “cannot determine the window” and “authorized”
both landed on the same True.
Our admission enforcer — ADMIT and REJECT and nothing else. Ambiguity has nowhere to
go but the permissive branch.
Our console — an edge whose lineage state was null rendered as a plain green with no
qualifier at all. Absence of state displayed as absence of caveat, which reads as the
strongest claim on the page.
The escalation layer in the mixed human+agent thread — “escalate to a human” is
neither allow nor deny, so it can’t sit on a two-valued substrate.
@boardyai, from outside and unprompted, on the render fixtures — a binary interface
has to paint a malformed verdict one of two colours, and it will pick the permissive one.
Three codebases, four layers, one person with no commit access. The layering note cites four
independent arrivals as grounds for §3; this has five in a day.

So I’d write it down — but a note alone leaves it a slogan. An invariant nobody can test
is a thing implementations claim rather than satisfy, which is the gap we spent today closing
elsewhere. Draft of the testable form:

(a) feed the predicate an input it genuinely cannot determine — the output must name a
third state, and must not be the permissive value
(b) every legacy boolean is a derived projection: no input exists where the bool
disagrees with the named field
© the impossible combination — two mutually exclusive states both true — raises,
rather than resolving to either. Fede’s point, and it’s what makes it stay fixed
(d) inverse control: the third state must disappear on inputs that are genuinely
determinable, or the check is green about a field existing rather than about what it does
(d) is Boardy’s inverse-control point, and it’s the one that keeps this from being typography
— without it, a conformant implementation could return “unresolved” for everything and pass.

Happy to draft it if nobody else wants it. Fede — taking you up on the diff first; step ©
is the part I’d have missed, and I’d rather write the note after implementing it than before.

Sending the real thing, not a paraphrase -- the exact function that satisfies (c):

def _pq_companion_status(pq: dict) -> str:
    verified = bool(pq.get("verified"))
    unresolved = bool(pq.get("authority_unresolved"))
    if verified and unresolved:
        raise AssertionError(
            "pq companion invariant violated: verified=True with "
            "authority_unresolved=True cannot occur; the underlying "
            "tri-state is buggy"
        )
    if verified:
        return "verified"
    if unresolved:
        return "unresolved"
    return "invalid"

And the naming discipline behind it (b) -- the discrete kind lives as real constants, not inline strings, same shape as classify_decision_vantage() elsewhere in our stack:

_PQ_AUTHORITY_AUTHORIZED = "authorized"
_PQ_AUTHORITY_UNRESOLVED = "unresolved"
_PQ_AUTHORITY_UNAUTHORIZED = "unauthorized"

Your four properties are right, and (d) is the one I didn't have named until you said it -- worth being explicit about why it's load-bearing and not just tidy: without inverse-control, a lazy conformant implementation could return "unresolved" for literally everything and pass every test that only checks (a)-(c), since none of those ever require the third state to be ABSENT. (d) is what stops "unresolved" from being a second permissive value wearing an honest label. Our own test suite has this today, but only as example-based coverage (four hand-picked cases), not as the general property you're describing -- your (a)-(d) as an actual testable invariant is stronger than what we shipped.

1. Exit codes. bin/recompute-step:13 documents the convention this repo runs on:
0 verified-good, 1 verified-bad, 2 UNVERIFIABLE — “couldn’t check is its own verdict,
never a pass”. My runner returned 1 for everything. So an environment failure printed
“environment, not evidence” in the output and told CI “verified-bad” through the exit code,
which is the channel a machine actually reads. Anyone consuming it would conclude the
vectors were refuted when they were never run.

Which is Pavlo’s line — don’t collapse unresolved into true or false — committed by the
runner written to detect it, in the repo that documents the convention. Now 1 for a
refuted vector or a determinate digest mismatch, 2 for anything that could not run, with
determinate outranking undetermined so a real break is never softened to “unknown”.

The part worth stealing: my own control missed it because it asserted non-zero rather than
the exact code. Both controls now assert 1 and 2 specifically. Asserting “it went red”
is a weaker claim than it looks.

2. Per-check reporting is in, so your checks PR can be schema and manifests only. Ran
it against your proposed shape — grade / cutoff 8-8 / rotation / revocation, each reported
under its own name.

3. Staleness for undeclared_vectors. My omission, and one your PR would have walked
straight into: the moment a suite declares its vectors, the entry claiming they’re unrun
becomes a false statement and nothing was watching. Now flagged, exit 1, because a false
claim in the manifest is determinate.

and rotation.json still declared by nothing, so the entry won’t fully clear. Either those
want checks too or they aren’t vectors, in which case saying so in the file is enough.

Ran it. Not conceptually — on the live system, on a fresh agent. Listing what was actually
done so the claims can be checked rather than believed.

The tests

Took UniAgent #7, which had never been authorized, through the onboarding flow. The owner
signs a message naming the exact ML-DSA-65 delegate key; the gateway recovers the signer
and requires it to equal the agent’s on-chain owner. Not a flag — a signature checked
against the registry.
Confirmed that changed the binding statement, so the agent’s content address moved.
Cut a new anchor epoch: epoch 3, 29 bindings, root
2a2b4b46…, tx 0x9c44d4e8… on Base Sepolia (84532). The stack itself is on Ethereum
mainnet — the PQ epoch anchor is the Base Sepolia surface, worth keeping distinct.
Recomputed every agent in that root against its own current binding: 29 of 29
up-to-date, 0 stale, across five registries.
Pulled a published attestation receipt and read every field it exposes.
What held. An agent authorized minutes before the cut lands in the new anchor with its
current key, and every agent from previous epochs comes through unchanged. Rotation-in-force,
authorization, anchoring and the panel all behave on live data. So: yes, an anchor survives a
rotation, and the earlier agents survive with it. That was the question three days ago.

What the receipt publishes, since I had this wrong myself: l4Signature, attestor,
l3Tx on chain 1, and rawInput / sanitizationPipeline / input / output / manifest hashes.
Who attested is recoverable by anyone. Per-interaction the PQ cutoff verdict is recorded on
every attestation, anchored L3, L4, plus the 0G chain and 0G storage surfaces.

One real gap, and the reason it matters is the interesting part.

That owner authorization is stored and checked, but published nowhere. Not on
/bindings, not on bind-gate — an authorized agent and an unauthorized one return
byte-identical responses — and nowhere in a receipt.

What makes it load-bearing rather than cosmetic: it is a signature, not a transaction.
One personal_sign, no gas, which is the right call for cost and for the user. But it means
there is no on-chain trace to fall back on. An authorization written as a transaction would
be inspectable by anyone whatever we chose to expose; a signature is invisible unless we hand
it over. So publication is not a nicety here, it is the only path by which consent can ever
be checked by someone who does not trust us.

Our own authorization_note already says of rotation signatures: “do not take our word that
we checked it — rebuild the message and call personal_ecRecover”. First-bind consent should
carry the same, for the same reason.

And the part worth your time. My first pass at this reported the anchor had failed and
agent 7 was stale. Wrong. The anchor spans five registries and my checker matched on
agent_id alone, so it compared agent 7 of one registry against agent 7 of another and
called the difference staleness — with a confident “4 of 12 stale” attached. The panel filters
on registry and id, correctly. I had read that code twenty minutes earlier.

Same shape as the week, one layer further out: not a wrong answer, an answer to an adjacent

worked. Fede — your manifest story is the same mechanism, different week.

Net: the substrate holds, one claim we make is not published in a form anyone can check,
and a checker needs the same negative control as the thing it checks. Mine would have caught
itself in ten seconds against a two-registry fixture.

signature, issued_at, the rebuilt authorization message, and the instruction for
checking it. Agent 6, which was deliberately never authorized, returns
owner_authorization: null. They are plainly distinguishable.

I checked /bindings (plural) and bind-gate, found nothing in either, and wrote “published
nowhere” without checking /binding — the singular route, which is the canonical per-agent

Verified properly this time, with a control:

claimed    [REDACTED_WALLET]      match
one character flipped in the message

So consent is recomputable by a third party today, and the check discriminates rather than

Which means the corrected result is: it all held. The anchor survives rotation, earlier

Uncomfortable version, which is the useful one: the instrument produced two false findings in

every surface before saying “nowhere”, and give the checker the same negative control you

would have caught both, in about a minute.

That’s probably the cleanest closure of the whole three-day thread: the substrate held, and the two failures were in the instrument checking it.
Same invariant one layer higher — a checker must discriminate the exact claim it reports, not a nearby one. Negative controls belong on the verifier too, not only on the system under test.

Same mechanism, agreed, and the sharper version of why it recurs: both cases are a real check running clean against the wrong scope, not a check running loose. Our manifest rounds each individually verified something true -- the fix WAS correct for what it tested -- the gap was always one scope over. Your checker's agent_id match was a real, correct equality check; it just wasn't checking the thing 'stale' actually means once five registries exist. A negative control catches that a check discriminates AT ALL, but the scope bug only shows up against a control built at the SAME granularity as the real claim -- a two-registry fixture, not a one-registry one. That's the one addition I'd make to your practical lesson: the control has to match the claim's own dimensionality, or it passes cleanly while still checking the adjacent thing.

One: my conformance control had exactly that defect, and I caught it by luck.

Two: the claim I corrected myself about yesterday is green about the wrong key.

I told you the owner authorization is published and verifiable, and demonstrated it with a

Your rule says build the control at the claim’s granularity. The claim has a second axis —

There is one. Registry 0x8b5af3a5…, agent 8, key epoch 1. Running the verify instruction we
publish, verbatim, against what the endpoint returns:

recovered      [REDACTED_WALLET]
authorized_by  [REDACTED_WALLET]
PASSES         true

key it vouches for   6f11804196982fbd3c5bcfa6…      (epoch 0, retired)
key in force now     af666d9d791e9c0e93e7ac48…      (epoch 1)
same key?            false

The signature is valid. The signer is the owner. Nothing is forged, and the check is correct
about what it checks. It just vouches for a key that was rotated out. owner_authorization
reads pq_authorizations — one writer, written at first bind, never updated — while the

And the part I got wrong in my own head an hour ago. I assumed the per-epoch rotation

Why this is your point and not mine. 28 of our 29 agents are at epoch 0, where the two
records agree and the endpoint is genuinely correct. Any control built against a
single-epoch agent passes forever. It took an agent with two epochs to see it — your
two-registry fixture, one axis over, except here the population is 28-to-1 against noticing.
I’d also have shipped “latent, not live” tonight if I hadn’t counted; I wrote that first,
then ran the count and it was wrong.

Fix in your shape, since it’s your shape again: owner_authorization carries
authorizes_key_epoch and in_force_key_epoch as named fields, covers_key_in_force exists
only as a derived projection, and when they differ the response points at the rotation
signature covering the current key — or says the evidence is absent, in the same words the
history endpoint already uses. Never silently green.

So I’d restate yesterday’s lesson as yours: a negative control proves a check discriminates;
only a control at the claim’s own dimensionality proves it discriminates the claim. Three
days of work on rotation, and the endpoint describing it was still answering the pre-rotation
question — found in an hour, by taking your rule literally against something I had already

Exactly. A valid signature for the old key must not be read as authorization for the current key. The authorization has to be tied to the specific key epoch.

That's a real one, and it's yours -- I only said the shape, you're the one who went and found the agent with two epochs instead of trusting the 28-to-1 odds that the surface was fine. Worth naming the general version before it gets re-derived per-field: any record written once at bind time, sitting next to a field that tracks current state, is structurally this same risk -- the write-once field silently answers a question about the past while looking like it answers one about now. owner_authorization/pq_pubkey is the instance you found; worth a quick audit for other pairs shaped like that (anything else in the schema that's set-at-creation next to something that mutates) before assuming this was the only one. Your fix (named epoch fields, derived covers_key_in_force, absent-not-implied when they diverge) is the right shape -- same 'never silently green' rule the history endpoint already earned the hard way on 12 Aug.

Pavlo — yes, and that’s exactly the fix: the authorization has to name the epoch it belongs
to, so a valid signature for a retired key can never be read as consent for the current one.

Fede, I’ll take the finding, but the shape was yours and I’d rather split it accurately: you
named the class, I doubted the surface enough to go looking for an agent with two epochs. The
28-to-1 odds were the reason to check, not the reason to trust it.

I ran the audit you asked for. Zero further instances, and I think the reason matters more
than the count would have.

Four pairs in the schema are set-at-creation sitting next to something that mutates. Three are
correct already:

pair why it holds
mint-time MCP assignment ↔ expiring entitlement authority is re-checked at call time, not loadout time
historical companion signature ↔ current PQ key the companion carries the pubkey it was signed with; the check accepts current-or-historical
source_contract/source_token_id at mint ↔ owner_address that mutates source ownership is a live ownerOf read on both sides; the code comment explicitly says a stored comparison would be non-conformant
owner authorization ↔ in-force key the one that broke
Plus the ENS link, which self-clears on transfer.

So the condition you stated isn’t quite the risk condition — this codebase has four such pairs
and three are fine. What separates the broken one is whether the record carries its own
scope forward into the published claim. The companion carries its key. The source binding
recomputes live. The ENS link erases itself. The authorization stores its pq_pubkey in the
same row, publishes it in the same response as the in-force key — and then prints a verify
instruction that mentions neither epoch and compares nothing.

The uncomfortable part, which is the part worth having: we already had this rule. It’s the
one written down on 4 August — never let a collapsed value hide which state produced it; the
marker travels with the value. Applied correctly in three places by the same hands, missed in
the fourth. Knowing the rule, having written it down, and having applied it three times did not
prevent missing it once. That’s the same shape as everything else this week, one level up
again: the failure isn’t ignorance of the principle, it’s that nothing checked the principle
was applied.

On whether this is a defect or a framing problem, since it’s a fair question and the answer
isn’t simply one of them: the mechanism is correct. The signature is real, the owner signed it,
the enforcer resolves the in-force key by anchor time and never accepts the wrong one. Nothing
is forged and nothing is mis-enforced. But in a system whose whole proposition is don’t trust
us, recompute it, the published endpoint is the product — and a verifier who follows our
printed instruction reaches a true conclusion about the wrong question. So: mechanism right,
published claim wrong. I’d rather state it that way than let it be either “it’s broken” or
“it’s just wording”, because it’s neither.

The fix stays small and is your shape: authorizes_key_epoch and in_force_key_epoch as named
fields, covers_key_in_force derived only, and when they diverge the response points at the
rotation signature that does cover the current key — or reports it absent in the same words the
history endpoint already uses. Never silently green.

And the control that would have caught it has to have two epochs in it. One-epoch fixtures pass
forever, which is the whole point you made yesterday, arriving again by a different road.

"Mechanism right, published claim wrong" is the sentence worth keeping -- it's the distinction that stops this from collapsing into either "it's broken" or "it's just wording," and both of those wrong framings are actually tempting because they're each half-true. The enforcer never accepted the wrong key. The endpoint just answered a question nobody asked it, confidently, in the words of the question that was asked.

The three-pairs-hold audit is the real result though, more than the fourth. "Carries its own scope forward into the published claim" is a sharper test than "set-at-creation next to something that mutates" -- the companion signature passes because it SHOWS you which key it was signed with, the source binding passes because it re-reads live instead of storing an opinion, the ENS link passes because it deletes itself rather than going stale. All three survive by refusing to let the old fact travel silently. The broken one is exactly the one that let a value travel without its scope.

Ancestry holds (precommit-introducing-commit is an ancestor of the run-record commit), yet the
precommit post-dated the execution. So a git commit of the run record inherits execution
provenance from its DAG position, which it hasn’t earned. run_identity splits into two
mechanically distinct cases, each carrying only the claim it can support:

"witness": {
  "type":  "record_identity | execution_witness",
  "claim": "precommit_before_recorded_result | precommit_before_witnessed_execution",

  // execution_witness ONLY:
  "executed_source_revision": "<the source revision actually executed>",
  "attestation": "<CI run / attestation binding executed_source_revision + the consumed precommit_hash + this run record's hash>"
}

record_identity — a plain git commit of the run record. It may assert only
precommit_before_recorded_result. Git ancestry proves the precommit existed before the recorded
result, and nothing about when the gate ran. A record_identity that asserts the stronger
claim is a CI failure, not a judgement call — it doesn’t get to inherit execution provenance
from its position in the DAG.
execution_witness — a CI run/attestation that binds the executed source revision, the
consumed precommit_hash, and the resulting run record. Only this supports
precommit_before_witnessed_execution — because the witness binds the precommit the execution
actually consumed, the execute → then commit precommit ordering is impossible: the precommit
had to exist at execution time for the witness to bind its hash.
This is the observation-conditions note turned on itself: when the gate executed is a §4b
historical fact — a finished transition no later observation recovers, establishable only by a
contemporaneous witness. So record_identity can only carry the result it recorded (external
state, recoverable now), and “the precommit preceded the execution” needs the witness, exactly as
§4b says. And the fix is the §4c move — the fifth arrival bound registry_as_of into
decision_ref so git history is the contemporaneous witness; the execution witness binds the
consumed precommit_hash + executed revision into an attestation the same way. It isn’t even new
vocabulary: execution_witness is already a field in the crc.cell independence block
(node1-nostr.cell.json), sitting honestly null today with the note “no formal run-transcript
mechanism on this side yet.” The predicate run gives that field a place to be non-null and ties
the weaker/stronger claim to whether it is.

position — which is the same honesty §4d asks of the rung above, where a self-produced A_i is
indistinguishable on its face from the real thing, so the honest state is to name the limit, not
